This topic goes one level deeper into the actual REPRESENTATION of missingness in Python and pandas, since None, NaN, NaT, and pd.NA are all different objects with different behavior, and confusing them causes real bugs.

blocks.text: 2. NaN Is Not Equal To Itself
A genuinely surprising fact worth demonstrating directly: NaN violates the normal rule that a value equals itself.

code.content:
import numpy as np
print(np.nan == np.nan)   # False
print(np.nan is np.nan)   # True, same object, but == still returns False

blocks.text: np.nan cannot represent a missing INTEGER, since NaN forces the whole column to float64. pandas introduced pd.NA and nullable dtypes like Int64 (capital I) to work consistently across integer and boolean columns, which np.nan cannot do.

code.content:
s = pd.Series([1, 2, None, 4])
print(s.dtype)   # float64, silently converted even though every real value is a whole number

s2 = pd.array([1, 2, None, 4], dtype='Int64')
print(s2.dtype)  # Int64, the nullable integer type, stays a true integer column

blocks.text: Never use == None or == np.nan directly, because of the equality behavior shown above. Always use pd.isna() or pd.isnull(), which correctly detects None, NaN, and NaT all at once, and their opposite pd.notna().

code.content:
df['col'] == None       # WRONG, does not reliably detect missing values
pd.isna(df['col'])       # CORRECT, catches None, np.nan, and NaT consistently
df['col'].notna()        # the opposite, correctly detects present values

s = pd.Series(['a', None, np.nan, 'd'])
print(pd.isna(s))
# 0    False
# 1     True
# 2     True
# 3    False

blocks.text: fillna() replaces missing markers with a specific value. This is a mechanical operation distinct from the imputation STRATEGY discussed in the sibling topic, which is about choosing WHAT value to fill with.

blocks.title: A real bug pattern
blocks.content: A function checking `if value == None` will silently fail to catch a np.nan value sitting in the same column, letting a missing value slip through undetected.

items: Using == for null checks instead of pd.isna().
Not realizing an integer column silently became float64 after a single missing value was introduced.
Mixing pd.NA and np.nan in ways that behave inconsistently across pandas versions.
